three-classes.t: Now emails come in **three kinds**: personal, promotional or spam. This is **multiclass classification**: more than two classes, and each email still has **exactly one**.

input-example.t: A new email arrives with two features: **7 suspicious words** and **3 promotional words**. The model must choose one of the three classes.

class-scores.t: A common design gives **one score per class**: personal 0.5, promotional 1.2, spam 2.1. These are **raw scores, not yet probabilities**.

compare-scores.t: Compare the three scores with each other: **2.1 beats 1.2 beats 0.5**. No single threshold is involved; the classes **compete**.

probabilities.t: **Softmax** turns the class scores into probabilities that sum to 1 and keeps the order: personal **0.126**, promotional **0.253**, spam **0.622**. Its purpose is just this conversion.

choose-largest.t: The predicted class is the one with the **largest probability**: spam. A class can win with less than 0.5, for example 0.40 against 0.35 and 0.25.

decision-regions.t: In feature space each class **owns a region**, and the boundaries meet between regions. Our email lands in the **spam region**.

ml-example.t: Two ways to build it: **one-versus-rest** trains one binary classifier per class and picks the most confident, while **a single model with class scores and softmax** compares all classes at once. Both predict exactly one class.
